subsection: 7. Case study: the Oil Crisis, 1973, and the Western economies, 1973–1990; Margaret Thatcher

notes.h: Background: the post-war boom and its weak points
notes.b: The oil crisis struck an economy that had grown rapidly for almost thirty years on cheap energy and stable exchange rates. To judge how much damage the shock did, you need to know what was already shaky before October 1973.
points: From 1945 to 1973 Western Europe enjoyed a post-war boom of rapid growth, full employment, Marshall Aid (American money for rebuilding), free trade and a growing welfare state. People came to expect that prosperity would simply continue.

Keynesian economics was the guiding idea: governments should manage demand, by spending more or cutting taxes, to keep employment high. In Britain it produced a post-war 'consensus', meaning both main parties accepted full employment and the welfare state.

Western European oil consumption had risen sharply since the 1950s, and most imported oil came from the Middle East. Oil became the main energy source in the 1950s and 1960s, supplying around half or more of Western Europe's energy by 1973.
Oil was bought cheaply in dollars, at about three dollars a barrel in 1973. Because economies were built around cheap oil, any large price rise would hit every importing country.

The Bretton Woods system fixed exchange rates, so that currencies kept a stable value against the dollar. It collapsed in 1971–73, when the USA ended dollar convertibility to gold in August 1971, and currency values became less predictable.
Inflation, a general rise in prices, had begun to rise in the late 1960s. This is why many historians argue the boom was already weakening before the oil shock.
notes.tip: Examiners reward essays that separate the oil shock from other causes of the end of the boom. Name inflation and the collapse of Bretton Woods as earlier weaknesses.

notes.h: Background: the Arab–Israeli conflict and the oil producers
notes.b: The oil shock was a political act as much as an economic one. Arab oil producers had grievances over prices and over land Israel held, and in 1973 they found a way to turn oil into a weapon.
points: Israel was created in 1948, and the Arab–Israeli conflict that followed shaped Middle East politics for decades.

In the Six-Day War of June 1967 Israel occupied Sinai, Gaza, the West Bank, East Jerusalem and the Golan Heights. Arab states wanted this land back, so Israeli withdrawal from the occupied territories became the producers' main political demand.
OPEC (the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries) was formed in 1960 and includes producers of all regions. Its Arab members had long sought higher prices for their oil.
OAPEC (the Organisation of Arab Petroleum Exporting Countries) was formed in 1968 and includes Arab members only, so it could act on Arab political aims such as the occupied territories.
An 'oil shock' means a sudden, large rise in the price of oil that hits the economies importing it. The crisis of 1973 was the first of two such shocks.
notes.tip: Do not mix up the two organisations. OPEC (1960, all producers) raised prices, while OAPEC (1968, Arab members only) made the output cuts and embargo.

notes.h: The Yom Kippur War and the price rise, October 1973
notes.b: On 6 October 1973 the Arab–Israeli conflict turned into open war. Within two weeks the oil producers had used the war as the occasion to raise prices and cut supply.
points: The Yom Kippur War began on 6 October 1973 when Egypt and Syria attacked Israel. It was the trigger for the oil crisis.
The USA resupplied Israel with arms during the war. This led the Arab states to use oil as a weapon against supporters of Israel.

On 16 October 1973 OPEC's Gulf members raised the posted price (the official price set by the producers) by about 70 per cent. This rise affected every importing country, not just those later singled out.

On 17 October OAPEC announced output cuts of 5 per cent a month, to continue until Israel withdrew from the occupied territories. Cutting supply pushed prices up further because buyers competed for less oil.
notes.tip: Learn the dates: war on 6 October, price rise on 16 October, output cuts on 17 October. At Ordinary Level, one correct dated statement earns a mark.

notes.b: The embargo was aimed at particular countries, while the price rise hit everyone. Together they ended the era of cheap oil.
points: An embargo is a ban on supplying particular countries. One was placed on oil exports to the USA from 19–20 October 1973 and on the Netherlands from 21 October, as supporters of Israel.
The Netherlands was targeted because its government supported Israel and because Rotterdam was Europe's main oil port, so cutting it off hurt Europe's whole supply network.
The Yom Kippur War ended with a ceasefire in late October 1973, following UN Security Council Resolution 338 of 22 October. Western governments then reassessed their dependence on imported energy.
The price was raised again at the end of 1973. Taken with the October rise, this meant that by early 1974 oil cost about four times its pre-war price, so prices roughly quadrupled.
The embargo was lifted in March 1974, but the new higher prices stayed in place. This is why the economic damage outlasted the political crisis.
notes.tip: The Netherlands was embargoed, but all importers faced the price rise. Say 'prices roughly quadrupled' rather than claiming the December increase was a doubling.

notes.b: Governments and households reacted to shortages and soaring prices by using less fuel. The measures were visible and are easy to illustrate with named examples.
points: Car-free Sundays were introduced in the Netherlands and West Germany in the winter of 1973–74, so that private motoring, a big user of petrol, was cut.
Governments reduced speed limits, because cars burn less fuel at lower speeds, and asked households to turn down their heating.
The Netherlands also issued ration coupons for petrol, so rationing is a Dutch example.

In Britain, Edward Heath's government introduced a three-day working week for industry from January to March 1974. A miners' overtime ban and dispute added to the power shortage, which cut electricity supplies.
notes.tip: If asked for rationing, name the Netherlands. Britain's emergency measure was the three-day week, not petrol rationing.

notes.h: Economic effects: inflation, deficits and stagflation
notes.b: Higher oil prices fed through the whole economy. Western Europe faced rising prices and falling output at the same time, a combination that its economic thinking had not prepared it for.
points: Inflation rose sharply, because oil is used in transport, heating and manufacturing, so higher energy costs pushed up the price of almost everything.
Industrial production fell and unemployment rose from the low levels of the 1960s, with the sharpest increases in heavy industry.
The balance of payments of oil-importing states went into deficit. That means they paid out more for imports than they earned from exports, because they now had to pay far more for oil.
The Arab producers gained huge revenues, known as petrodollars (oil income in dollars), which were recycled through Western banks.
Stagflation is the combination of stagnation (no growth, falling output and rising unemployment) with rising prices. It is different from an ordinary recession and from inflation on its own.
Conventional Keynesian policies struggled with stagflation. Boosting demand to cut unemployment would push prices up further, but cutting demand to reduce inflation would deepen unemployment.
notes.tip: Exams ask why Keynesian remedies struggled: each cure for one problem made the other worse. Define stagflation as stagnation plus rising prices.

notes.h: The second oil shock and mass unemployment
notes.b: A second shock in 1979 meant the first was not a one-off. Together they produced the long recession and unemployment of the early 1980s.
points: The Iranian revolution of 1979 caused the second oil shock, which is different from the first shock of 1973–74 that followed the Yom Kippur War. Oil prices roughly doubled between 1978 and 1980.
The second shock pushed many economies back into a second recession in 1980–82, just as they were recovering from the first.
Unemployment across the EEC rose from low levels in the early 1970s to above 10 per cent by the mid-1980s. Spain and Ireland suffered much higher rates.
The rise was worst in heavy industry and in the north of Britain, Scotland and Wales, where coal, steel and shipbuilding were concentrated. British unemployment reached about three million in 1982.
Riots in English cities in 1981, including Brixton and Toxteth, came during this period of recession.
Rising unemployment also strained the welfare state, because more people needed benefits while fewer paid taxes.
notes.tip: For cause-and-result questions on why unemployment rose, link the 1973 shock, the 1979 shock and the decline of heavy industry. Keep the two shocks apart by date and cause.

notes.b: Recession and costly energy exposed industries that could no longer compete. The result was deindustrialisation, the long-term decline of manufacturing and heavy industry and the jobs it provided.
points: Britain's steel, coal and shipbuilding industries declined sharply, and the loss of these jobs changed the regional economies of the north and Scotland.
Older industries such as coal, steel and shipbuilding were cut back across Europe, because demand fell and competitors elsewhere produced more cheaply.
The EEC introduced steel quotas in 1980, known as the Davignon Plan after Étienne Davignon, the commissioner for industry. Quotas limited how much steel each producer could make.
West Germany contrasts with Britain: its industry moved up-market into machinery and cars, which kept it competitive.
notes.tip: Remember the contrast. Britain lost heavy industry, while West Germany moved up-market. Name the Davignon Plan and 1980 for steel.

notes.b: The shock made energy independence a political goal. Governments looked for new sources and for ways to use less oil.
points: France announced a nuclear power programme in 1974, the Messmer Plan, named after Prime Minister Pierre Messmer. By the late 1980s nuclear power gave about 70 per cent of French electricity.
North Sea oil began to flow in the mid-1970s. By about 1980 Britain was self-sufficient in oil and Norway a major exporter, which cushioned both economies against the second oil shock.
The International Energy Agency was set up in 1974 under the OECD to coordinate oil stocks and policy among importing states.
Energy conservation and the development of coal and nuclear power were promoted as ways to reduce dependence on imported oil.
notes.tip: Name one policy per country: Messmer Plan for France, North Sea oil for Britain and Norway, and the International Energy Agency (1974) for cooperation.

notes.h: Significance of the Oil Crisis and differing views
notes.b: The crisis ended the long boom, but historians disagree about how much of that was the oil shock's doing. Examiners ask how lasting the impact was.
points: The crisis ended the long boom and exposed the dependence of Western prosperity on cheap energy. It shifted political attention from growth to inflation and unemployment.
It strengthened the case for the EEC to act together, leading to the European Monetary System in 1979. There is more on this in the notes on European unity.
Contemporaries blamed the Arab embargo and OPEC for the economic troubles.

Many economists later argued that inflation, the end of Bretton Woods and falling productivity were already weakening the boom, so the oil shock hastened the end of the boom rather than solely causing it.
The embargo also gave oil-producing states a new role in world politics and led Western states to look for energy independence, through nuclear power, North Sea oil and conservation.
Its impact was lasting in some ways, as energy policy changed. Unemployment and industrial decline also remained long after the embargo ended.
notes.tip: Never write that the oil crisis caused the end of the boom as a flat statement. Say it hastened an already weakening boom, and name the other causes.

notes.h: Key concepts: capitalism, welfare state, monetarism and privatisation
notes.b: Thatcher's policies make sense only against a few ideas. These terms are used throughout the rest of the notes, so each is defined as it applies to this period.
points: Capitalism is an economic system based on private ownership, competitive markets and profit. Thatcher's aim was to extend it, through privatisation and free markets.

The welfare state is state provision of health, pensions, benefits and education. It was strained by unemployment and cost after 1973. Thatcher cut the growth in spending but did not dismantle its core.
Monetarism is the policy of controlling inflation by controlling the money supply, the amount of money circulating in the economy. It is the opposite of Keynesianism, which manages demand.
Privatisation means selling state-owned firms to private owners. Deregulation is different: it means removing rules, as in the City of London in 1986.
Trade union laws were the Employment Acts of 1980 and 1982 and the Trade Union Act of 1984, which limited union power.
notes.tip: Examiners expect these terms to be used accurately. Keep monetarism (money supply) apart from Keynesianism (demand), and privatisation (selling firms) apart from deregulation (removing rules).

notes.b: Thatcher led the Conservative Party from 1975 and was Prime Minister from 1979 to 1990, pursuing monetarist and free-market policies. She was a direct participant in almost every episode that follows, as well as someone shaped by the failures of the 1970s.
points: She was born in Grantham on 13 October 1925, the daughter of a grocer, Alfred Roberts. She studied chemistry at Somerville College, Oxford, and was called to the bar in 1953, so she was a barrister, before becoming MP for Finchley in 1959.
She was Secretary of State for Education and Science in Edward Heath's government from 1970 to 1974.

Heath lost two general elections in 1974, in February and October, and her break with him followed. Keith Joseph, whose policy ideas lay behind monetarism, founded the Centre for Policy Studies in 1974 with her.
On 11 February 1975 she was elected Conservative leader. Heath was knocked out in the first ballot, and she then won the second ballot against Willie Whitelaw.
She became Prime Minister on 4 May 1979, defeating James Callaghan's Labour government after the 1978–79 'winter of discontent'. Note that she was leader from 1975 but Prime Minister only from 1979.
She won the general elections of 1979, 1983 and 1987. Her term of about eleven and a half years was the longest continuous premiership of the twentieth century.
She was shaped by Heath's failure, the crisis of the 1970s and Joseph's ideas, and shaped events as Prime Minister in every episode that follows.
notes.tip: Do not say 'she defeated Edward Heath' as if one ballot decided it, and mention both 1974 elections when explaining her rise.

notes.b: Thatcher's central aim was to defeat inflation, even at the cost of unemployment. Her government used monetarism to do so, and the results were mixed.
points: Her Chancellor, Geoffrey Howe, applied monetarism, an approach associated with Milton Friedman. The Medium Term Financial Strategy (1980) was the plan for cutting inflation by controlling the money supply.
Howe's 1981 budget raised taxes in the middle of a recession, which shocked many experts: 364 economists signed a letter of protest.
Inflation fell from double figures in 1980, about 18 per cent, to under 5 per cent by 1983, so the main aim was achieved.
Unemployment passed three million in 1982, and the early 1980s recession hit manufacturing in the north, Scotland and Wales hardest, with riots in English cities in 1981.
Under her government, fighting inflation replaced full employment as the main priority, which marked a break with the post-war consensus.
notes.tip: A top essay on Thatcher gives each point a date and a named policy. Pair the achievement (inflation down by 1983) with its cost (unemployment over three million in 1982).

notes.h: Thatcher: privatisation, deregulation and the union laws
notes.b: Thatcher wanted a freer market economy with less state ownership and weaker unions. Her government passed a series of measures between 1979 and 1986 to achieve it.
points: Exchange controls, which had limited moving money abroad, were abolished in October 1979.
The Housing Act 1980 gave council tenants a right to buy their homes, spreading property ownership.
Privatisation sold state assets to private owners: British Telecom in 1984, British Gas in 1986 and British Airways in 1987.
The City of London was deregulated in October 1986, the 'Big Bang', when old rules were removed from financial trading. This was deregulation, not privatisation.
The Employment Act 1980 limited secondary picketing (pickets at a workplace not involved in the dispute) and restricted the closed shop (a workplace where all workers must join the union).
The Employment Act 1982 added further limits on the closed shop and made unions liable for damages, so unions risked heavy costs when strikes broke the law.
The Trade Union Act 1984 required secret ballots for strikes and for union executives.
notes.tip: Be exact with the three union laws: Employment Acts 1980 and 1982, Trade Union Act 1984. Do not confuse privatisation (British Telecom, 1984) with deregulation (the City, 1986).

notes.b: The Falklands War gave Thatcher a victory at a time when her policies had made her unpopular. It helped to transform her political position.
points: Argentina invaded the Falklands on 2 April 1982. Thatcher sent a task force, and Argentine forces surrendered on 14 June 1982.
She was the Prime Minister who sent the task force, not a combatant, so describe her as the leader who took the decision.
Her popularity recovered, and she won a landslide in the general election of June 1983.
notes.tip: If you write on the Falklands, give both dates, 2 April and 14 June 1982, and link the victory to her 1983 landslide.

notes.b: The strike was the most severe test of Thatcher's trade union policy. It followed the pit closure plans of the National Coal Board and ended in defeat for the miners.
points: The strike began in March 1984 with the announcement of the closure of the Cortonwood pit, when the National Coal Board chairman, Ian MacGregor, announced a closure programme.
Arthur Scargill's National Union of Mineworkers called the strike without holding a national ballot.
The government had built up coal stocks, so power supplies could continue, and it used mass policing. Violent clashes occurred at Orgreave on 18 June 1984.
The miners returned to work in March 1985 without a settlement. The defeat weakened the union movement and speeded up the closure of coal mines.
notes.tip: Examiners ask why the miners lost. Use the government's coal stocks, mass policing and the lack of a national ballot. Do not confuse Orgreave (the June 1984 clash) with Cortonwood (the pit that started the strike).

notes.h: Thatcher, the USA, the USSR and Northern Ireland
notes.b: Abroad, Thatcher combined a close alliance with the USA with a cautious readiness to deal with the Soviet Union. She also signed a significant agreement on Northern Ireland.
points: Her relationship with President Ronald Reagan was close, and the two leaders coordinated the Western response to Soviet policy in the early 1980s.
US cruise missiles were deployed at Greenham Common from 1983, and US aircraft flew from British bases in the raid on Libya in April 1986. Both showed her support for Reagan.
A Soviet newspaper nicknamed her the 'Iron Lady' in January 1976. She later adopted the name with some pride.
She met Mikhail Gorbachev at Chequers in December 1984, before he took power, and said he was a man she could 'do business with'. She then helped to persuade Reagan that he was sincere.
She signed the Anglo-Irish Agreement with the Taoiseach, Garret FitzGerald, at Hillsborough on 15 November 1985. It gave the Irish government a consultative role in Northern Ireland.
notes.tip: Do not confuse Greenham Common (cruise missiles) with the Libya raid (April 1986). Both are examples of her support for Reagan.

notes.b: Thatcher backed the EEC as a market but resisted its move towards political union. Her attitude shows in a run of dated episodes.
points: She negotiated the British budget rebate at the Fontainebleau European Council in June 1984, which reduced Britain's net contribution to the EEC budget. This showed her hard line on money.
She approved the Single European Act in 1986 because it supported the single market, a free market in goods and services across the EEC.
In her Bruges speech of 20 September 1988 she criticised plans for a federal Europe while supporting a single market.
She opposed the Social Charter and economic and monetary union.
Britain joined the Exchange Rate Mechanism only in October 1990, shortly before her fall.
notes.tip: State her attitude directly: supporter of the single market, opponent of federalism. Support it with Fontainebleau (1984, rebate), the Single European Act (1986) and Bruges (1988). Maastricht came in 1992, after her fall.

notes.b: Thatcher won three elections but was removed by her own party. Europe and the poll tax were the underlying causes.
points: The poll tax (Community Charge), a flat-rate local tax, was introduced in Scotland in 1989 and in England and Wales in 1990. It became a major cause of the challenge to her.
Geoffrey Howe resigned on 1 November 1990 over her European policy, and he made a critical speech on 13 November.
Michael Heseltine then challenged her for the leadership. She won the first ballot on 20 November 1990 but not by the margin required, so the contest was not settled.
She announced her resignation on 22 November 1990 and left office on 28 November, when John Major succeeded her.
notes.tip: Say 'announced her resignation on 22 November' and 'left office on 28 November'. Examiners ask why she fell, so link Howe, Heseltine, Europe and the poll tax.

notes.b: Judgements on Thatcher were sharply divided at the time and remain so. You need both sides, as examiners reward a balanced verdict.
points: Admirers praised her resolve and credited her with ending the 'British disease' of industrial conflict and decline.
Critics pointed to unemployment passing three million in 1982, deindustrialisation, social division and the North–South gap. They also pointed to the poll tax.

Historians debate whether her policies were a decisive break with the post-war settlement or the continuation of trends already under way, such as the oil shock, the decline of heavy industry and the rise of finance.
'Thatcherism', her combination of free markets, privatisation and union reform, is seen as a lasting legacy.
notes.tip: Use 'supporters' and 'critics' rather than naming historians. Take a stated side on break or continuity.

notes.h: Assessment: the Oil Crisis, the 1970s and 1980s, and Thatcher
notes.b: The record of the Western economies after 1973 is judged on whether they restored growth and whether the costs of adjustment were fair. Thatcher's record is judged the same way.
points: Achievements: inflation was reduced, trade union power was curbed, privatisation and a more flexible labour market in Britain followed, and Britain's profile rose in Europe and with the USA, and the single market deepened in the EEC after 1986.
Limits: mass unemployment, the decline of manufacturing and mining communities, regional inequality, the poll tax and her fall in 1990.
Supporters of Thatcher say she reversed Britain's relative decline, while critics say the decline of manufacturing was a heavy and lasting cost.

The oil shock hastened the end of the boom but did not solely cause it, since inflation and industrial change were already under way. Its energy impact was lasting, but unemployment and industrial decline remained.

Contemporaries blamed the embargo and OPEC, while later economists stress earlier weaknesses. Contemporaries saw Thatcher as either resolute or divisive, while historians ask whether she broke with or continued earlier trends.
notes.tip: For a 100-mark Higher essay on Thatcher, state a judgement and balance achievements against costs, giving each point a date and a named policy.

keyTerms.definition: An economic system in which private owners run businesses for profit in competitive markets, which Thatcher's government sought to strengthen.
A system in which the state provides health care, pensions, unemployment benefit and education to citizens, funded mainly through taxation and insurance.
A combination of stagnant output, high unemployment and rising prices, which challenged conventional economic policy in the 1970s.
The economic doctrine that controlling the money supply is the key to controlling inflation, which Thatcher's government adopted.
The sale of state-owned companies to private owners, such as British Telecom in 1984.
The decline of manufacturing and heavy industry as a share of an economy's output and employment.
The Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries, formed in 1960, whose members set oil prices and output; its price rises of 1973 and 1979 caused the oil shocks.
A sudden and large rise in the price of oil, as in 1973–74 and 1979, which raised costs and inflation in importing countries.
Thatcher's Employment Acts of 1980 and 1982 and Trade Union Act of 1984, which restricted secondary picketing and the closed shop and required ballots.

factCards.term: Yom Kippur War: start and ceasefire
factCards.definition: The war began on 6 October 1973 when Egypt and Syria attacked Israel, and a ceasefire took effect in late October.

factCards.term: OPEC price rise: date and size
factCards.definition: On 16 October 1973 Gulf OPEC members raised the posted oil price by about 70 per cent.
Arab producers announced output cuts on 17 October 1973 and imposed embargoes on the USA and the Netherlands from 19–21 October.
The Netherlands and West Germany introduced car-free Sundays during the winter of 1973–74 to save fuel.
Britain introduced a three-day working week for industry from January to March 1974.
In 1974 France announced a nuclear power programme to reduce dependence on imported oil.
She was elected leader on 11 February 1975, defeating Edward Heath.
She became Prime Minister on 4 May 1979 after the Conservatives won the general election.
Thatcher's legislation restricted trade union actions such as secondary picketing and closed shops.
The National Union of Mineworkers strike ran from March 1984 to March 1985.
Argentina invaded the Falklands on 2 April 1982, and Argentine forces surrendered on 14 June 1982.
Thatcher gave her speech criticising a federal Europe at Bruges on 20 September 1988.
She resigned as Prime Minister on 22 November 1990 after a leadership challenge.
Defeating inflation, privatising state industries such as British Telecom, and winning the Falklands War in 1982.
Mass unemployment in the early 1980s, the decline of manufacturing and mining communities, and the poll tax.
Fuel rationing, inflation, rising unemployment and a shift of energy policy towards nuclear power and North Sea oil.
